newsitem.title: USA: YEAREND - Latin America debt '97 outlook favorable.
newsitem.headline: YEAREND - Latin America debt '97 outlook favorable.

text.p: Expectations for stronger economic growth and lower inflation in Latin America will help boost returns on the region's Brady instruments in 1997, but emerging market experts said it will be hard to match the spectacular performance seen in 1996.
Indeed, they agreed that another 400 to 600 basis points of yield spread tightening against U.S. Treasuries as witnessed in 1996 is virtually a mathematical impossibility.

"I think that the prospect for the same degree of tightening next year is virtually nil in the Brady market," said Lawrence Goodman, head of Latin American Economic Research at Salomon Brothers Inc in New York.
Nonetheless, emerging market debt experts said there is still room for further spread narrowing.
Arturo Porzecanski, chief economist at ING Barings in New York, said he expects Latin American debt to tighten by about 150 to 200 basis points in 1997.
Meanwhile, Nikhil Dhaon, vice president at Morgan Stanley Asset Management, predicts spread tightening of 100 to 150, "allowing for a 17.5 percent return."
Porzecanski, among others, said a favorable economic and inflation outlook, along with ample global liquidity in 1997 should fuel further compression of spreads in 1997.
Among the risks to Latin American debt performance is a reversal in monetary policy stance in 1997 by Japan, Germany and the United States.

"If the liquidity cycle turns in Japan, Europe or the United States, for whatever reason then that obviously is a cause for concern," said Dhaon, who does not foresee any dramatic change in the first half of 1997.
But even if liquidity started to dry up, Dhaon said the impact on Latin American debt would not be as dramatic as people might think because countries' economies will be much stronger in 1997.

Given expectations for a benign global environment, sources said Latin American debt markets should continue to enjoy the entrance of new money from traditional U.S. high-yield funds or cross-over buyers as they search out higher yielding instruments and look to diversify holdings.

"The emerging market asset class still looks relatively cheap across the board," said Gary Evans, chief emerging market fixed income strategist at Lehman Brothers, who also believes emerging debt markets have another leg of tightening.

According to Evans, a BB-plus emerging market sovereign credit will provide investors with an extra 100 basis points over a comparably rated U.S. corporate debt issue. He said investors will pick up even greater yield as they move further down the credit spectrum.
Meanwhile, sources said a favorable global environment, along with strong investor demand, will lead to a rise in borrowings by both Latin American countries and corporations.

"Only a significant back-up in U.S. interest rates (like the 30-year bond over 7.0 percent) could stop the emerging market bond issuance tide in 1997," said John Lonski, senior economist at Moody's Investors Service Inc.
According to experts, Argentina will be the largest issuer in 1997 to visit the international capital markets as it needs to refinance about $10 billion of its maturing debt.
In addition, Latin countries tapping the international capital markets for the first time ever in 1997 will likely include Ecuador and Panama.
Sources said there may also be some room for improvement in sovereign credit quality.

"If Latin American nations continue to make economic and fiscal progress, countries like Argentina and Brazil-- both rated at B1 -- have a good shot at improving their creditworthiness," said Lonski of Moody's.
In the Brady market, Evans said Ecuador should provide the highest return in Latin America in 1997. "The credit fundamentals are moving in the right direction," he said.
Indeed, Ecuadoran debt instruments should benefit from the recently announced economic package, which calls for reform measures including a convertibility plan and privatizations of state-run firms.

Evans also said he favors Panama PDI bonds which could provide a 20 percent return in 1997. "We believe...the country's sovereign rating could come in at a BB or even BB-plus sometime next year. This could cause the bonds to tighten almost 100 basis points."
Argentina, some experts estimate, will also post favorable returns as the country increasingly moves along a growth path.
Brazilian debt, on the other hand, could suffer if President Fernando Henrique Cardoso's efforts to enact a constitutional amendment which would allow for his re-election fails.
Experts said the pace of economic and administrative reforms face a slowdown in the event Congress turns down this proposal to modify the Brazilian constitution.
While Mexican debt could post modest gains in the first part of 1997, sources said congressionial elections in July will pose some political risk and could lead to increased volatility.
"I think there could be some peso volatility, Mexican stock market and Brady bond volatility in the runup to very contested elections," said Porzecanski.
